To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we developed a novel strategy to engineer the mechanical property and bioactivity of electrospun vascular grafts for vascular tissue engineering.

we developed a method to blend low-molecular-weight elastic polymer into electrospun graft scaffolds, which improved the mechanical property and the loading capacity of VEGF and prolonged the release.
we developed a novel approach to engineer the micro/nanotexture, mechanical properties and biological cues of vascular grafts to promote in situ endothelialization and tissue formation.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of a novel approach for the engineering of the mechanical and biological characteristics of electrospun nanofibrous scaffolding materials for the in situ tissue engineering of vascular grafts, which is a promising approach to overcome the limitations of synthetic vascular grafts.
the development of novel micro/nanofibrus vascular grafts with improved biological and mechanical properties for in situ vascular graft remodeling.
developing a novel method to improve the mechanical and biological performance of electrospun vascular grafts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
LMW elastic blending is a promising approach to engineer the biological and mechanical property of electrospun vascular grafts for the purpose of in situ tissue engineering.

this study demonstrates that LMW elastomeric polymer blending is an effective approach to engineer the biological and mechanical properties of micro/nanoffibrous scaffolds to enhance the performance of in situ vascular tissue-engineered grafts.

the addition of LMW elastomer during the electrospinning process improves the mechanical and biological performance of micro/nanofi-brous vascular grafts, and the VEGF release from heparin-conjugated scaffolds can significantly enhance the endothelium formation, thus increasing the patency of vascular tissue engineering.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we developed an approach for in situ vascular engineering by blending low molecular weight (MW) elastic polymer into electrospun scaffolds to increase the conjugation sites for biomolecule binding.
the LMW elastic polymers can be used to improve the mechanical and biological performance of the vascular grafts, and thus increase the patency of the vascular graft.
LMW elastic polymers can be used as a new approach to engineer the properties of electrospun vascular grafts for vascular tissue engineering.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the addition of a low molecular weight (MW) elastic polymer (LMWEP) during electrospinning improves the elasticity of electrospun scaffolds.
the addition of LMW elastic polymer during electro-spinning improves both the mechanical property and the biological performance of vascular grafts.
LMW elastic polymers can be used in electrospun vascular scaffolds to improve the mechanical and biological performance.
